preamble: Denasalization of [ĩ] to oral [i]. In Middle French, vowels that had been nasalized before a nasal consonant lost their nasality when that consonant remained before a vowel, so Old French fine [ˈfĩnə] became [fin] and ligne [ˈlĩɲə] became [liɲ], while in closed syllables the nasal vowel survived and lowered (fin [fɛ̃]). In Lithuanian the old nasal vowels written with an ogonek, including į, were denasalized and survive as long oral vowels, so į is now [iː].

examples.note: Middle French denasalization before /n/ or /m/ followed by a vowel; the masculine fin, where the nasal closed the syllable, kept and lowered the nasal vowel as [fɛ̃].
The same denasalization before an intervocalic palatal nasal /ɲ/.

examples.from: Proto-Balto-Slavic *in 'into' > earlier Lithuanian nasal [ĩː], spelled į
examples.note: The ogonek letters were introduced for what were then nasal vowels; these have since denasalized, and į now stands for oral long [iː].
